title: "Under the Silver Lake" (2019) and post-modern art

commenti.body: I have a lot of love for this film, and to me the postmodernism you describe is one of the films many red herrings. Everything Sam does in the film is an attempt to reclaim some kind of identity after breaking up with his girlfriend. It isn't explicit, but there are a lot of little clues that the breakup was extremely traumatic for him. He distracts himself from the pain by having meaningless sex, uncovering "conspiracies", and >!possibly killing dogs!<. Sam doesn't know who he is outside of his previous relationship, so he gravitates towards anything that makes him feel important or powerful. It seems kind of trite to call this a breakup movie, but seeing it through that lens really opened it up for me.

I would say your perspective on post-modern novels is rather naive and incomplete. Postmodern literature is usually characterized by meta aspects as well as intertextuality either internally or with history/canon. It is somewhat deconstructionist in nature. Nothing in particular to do with large conspiratorial organizations or outsider protagonists

I don't care much about deconstruction or anything related to Derrida's thought. What I said is that the novels that I read both feature conspirations and weirdo protagonists/characters. Which is true, no matter if my perspective is actually naive or not.

"I think I have an overall grasp of the themes and style of the genre"

Just offering you some perspective mate
I brought up the conspiracy theme mostly because it was relevant to the movie. It obviously isn't all there is to postmodern literature. I mentioned Derrida because you said deconstruction.

Yeah I fail to find post-modernism in Under the Silver Lake. There are no meta aspects to it as far as I remember and maybe the most intertext is the owl cult conspiracy stuff, but that seems more like straightforward plot.

It's interesting that some people take this movie at face value and others as a clear story of mental illness. 

I didn't really take it as commentary on current generation. To me that's similar to casting an actor as representation of an ethnic group.

It is a fun exploration of the lines between obsession, neglect, limerence, and paranoia, and how those would pan out if such mind actually unearthed the secrets it always suspects around the corner.

If you want to dig deeper into this I'd suggest reading some Robert Anton Wilson.

You read two books and clearly did no other research I don't think that gives you the perspective to judge what postmodernism is. Those were similarities in the two books you read, not defining features of postmodernism.

However, there ARE similarities between Pynchon and Under the Silver Lake. Mainly in the sun drenched, surreal Los Angeles storytelling. Pynchon to an extent draws on the LA noir and hardboiled detective lit, and Under the Silver Lake heavily does, in it's very neo noir way. It reminded me a lot of the adaptation of Inherent Vice. I would say it is inspired by Pynchon as well as neo noirs, so it does have elements of postmodernism. 

I recommend reading other postmodernist books, there are so many great ones! Catch 22, anything by Kurt Vonnegut, Gabriel Garcia Marquez, Italo Calvino, Haruki Murakami...you might be interested in David Foster Wallace's essay on television and irony.
Hey fair enough mate, which Pynchon books did you read?
